guide.title: Vatican City: St Peter's, the Vatican Museums and the Sistine Chapel
guide.intro: Vatican City is a sovereign state. It is not one of Rome's rioni, it is not in Italy, and a traveller who walks up to St Peter's is entering another country. The Lateran Treaty, signed on 11 February 1929 and in force from the exchange of ratifications on 7 June 1929, created it, and the Governorate gives its area as 0.44 km2, or 44 hectares. Art. 3 of the Treaty states that St Peter's Square forms part of Vatican City, and it fixes the boundaries of the state only by the 1:5000 plan annexed to it as Allegato I. The Treaty describes the border in no other way. UNESCO inscribed Vatican City as a World Heritage property in 1984, under criteria (i)(ii)(iv)(vi) and at 44 hectares, separately from the Historic Centre of Rome.

sections.heading: The state and its institutions
sections.body:
The Governorate gives the area of the state as 0.44 km2, that is 44 hectares, partly surrounded by walls, and counts five entrances, guarded by the Pontifical Swiss Guard and the Corps of Gendarmerie. Access to the Vatican Museums is from Viale Vaticano. The Governorate records 673 citizens of the State, and, in statistics to 31 December 2024, 882 residents counting citizens and non-citizens. Of the citizens, 458 live inside the walls, among them 120 members of the Pontifical Swiss Guard, and some 30 per cent of citizens, mostly diplomatic staff, do not reside inside the State. The same statistics to 31 December 2024 give 66 cardinals who are Vatican citizens, ten of them living inside; six deaths in 2024; 21 squares; and 30 covered roads.

The Pontifical Swiss Guard was founded in 1506, and the Governorate says that according to tradition the uniforms were designed by Michelangelo. L'Osservatore Romano was founded in 1861 and the state has broadcast by radio since 1931. Vehicles carry the codes SCV, for the bodies of the State and the Holy See, and CV, for citizens and permit holders. The Holy See's postal form is 00120 Citta del Vaticano, and the Vatican Museums publish their own address, on the same street a visitor queues in, as Viale Vaticano, 00165 Rome.

The Governorate is the body through which the services of the state are run, and the Directorate of Museums and Cultural Heritage, which runs the Vatican Museums, sits under it. A small strip of Italian territory known as the Ricciolo d'Italia lies beside St Peter's Square. Its extent is not described in the Lateran Treaty, and in practice it is often treated as Vatican ground.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
The Vatican Museums give their own directions: Metro line A towards Battistini, stations Ottaviano or Cipro; bus 49, which stops in the square in front of the Museums; buses 32, 81 and 982 at Piazza del Risorgimento; buses 492 and 990 at Via Leone IV and Via degli Scipioni; tram 19 at Piazza del Risorgimento; and a taxi rank in the square in front of the Museums. The Museums entrance is on Viale Vaticano. St Peter's Basilica has a different door altogether, and the two are not the same visit.

The Fabbrica di San Pietro describes the way into the basilica plainly: access begins with the security checks by the Italian State Police, whose stations are in the right hemicycle of St Peter's Square looking towards the basilica. Entry to the basilica itself is free and needs no reservation, from the ordinary entrance in the square. Worshippers and celebrants have a dedicated route, with identification at an indicated entrance gate and staff accompaniment to prayer and celebration and then to the exit; anyone who wants to look round afterwards re-enters by the standard entrances.

A dress code applies across the Museums, the Sistine Chapel, St Peter's Basilica and the Vatican Gardens: no sleeveless or low-cut garments, no shorts above the knee, no miniskirts, no hats. The Museums cloakroom is free and compulsory for luggage, suitcases, rucksacks and packages, and for knives, scissors, metal tools, medium and large umbrellas, sticks, tripods, video cameras, banners and signs; visitors going on to the basilica are told not to leave baggage in the Museums.

sections.heading: Tickets, hours and closures
sections.body:
The Vatican Museums open Monday to Saturday from 08.00 to 20.00, with final entry at 18.00, and on the last Sunday of the month from 09.00 to 14.00, final entry 12.30, with free entry and guided tours on reservation, except where that Sunday falls on Easter Sunday, 29 June, 25 December, 26 December or 31 December. Visitors are asked to leave the halls 30 minutes before closing. The Museums are closed on Sundays other than the last of the month; on 1 and 6 January; 11 February; 19 March; 6 April; 1 May; 29 June; 14 and 15 August; 1 November; and 8, 25 and 26 December. The full ticket is 20.00 euro without online booking, or 20.00 plus 5.00 euro for Skip the Line booked on the official site; reduced is 10.00 euro plus 5.00; schools 5.00 plus 2.00; students, pilgrimages and university institutes 10.00 plus 5.00; seminaries and religious colleges 5.00 plus 2.00. The Museums state that tickets are sold online through tickets.museivaticani.va and warn that lookalike domains charge higher prices; a ticket admits to the Museums and the Sistine Chapel on the day it is issued, and is not refundable.

Entry to St Peter's Basilica is free and unreserved. The Fabbrica di San Pietro publishes basilica opening hours of 7.00 am to 8.00 pm from 1 June. Guided tours run Monday to Saturday 09.30 to 17.30, last registration 17.00, and on Sundays and Vatican holidays 13.30 to 15.30, last registration 15.00, with a themed tour on Bernini and the Barberini. The sacrament of Reconciliation is available Monday to Saturday 07.00 to 12.30 and 16.00 to 19.00, and Sunday 07.00 to 13.00 and 16.00 to 19.00, with continuous Eucharistic Adoration in the Chapel of the Blessed Sacrament from the end of the 08.30 Mass to the Benediction at day's end.

The dome is ticketed separately. The Fabbrica gives winter hours of 07.30 to 17.00 for 26 October 2025 to 28 March, and summer hours of 07.00 to 18.00 for 29 March 2026 to 25 October 2026, and the same ranges for the Petros eni exhibition. Its booking portal lists the dome with stairs, including the basilica, at 17 euro, and the dome with lift at 22 euro. The Vatican Gardens are sold as their own ticket category and are seen on a booked tour; the Necropolis of the Via Triumphalis is another, and the Vatican Necropolis under the basilica is visited by request through the Fabbrica. Tickets for General Audiences and for the Holy Father's liturgical celebrations are always free of charge: lay faithful request them from the Prefecture of the Papal Household, and bishops, priests and deacons from the Office for the Liturgical Celebrations of the Supreme Pontiff.

faq.question: Is St Peter's Square in Italy or in Vatican City?
faq.answer: Art. 3 of the Lateran Treaty says that St Peter's Square forms part of Vatican City, and adds that it continues to be normally open to the public. The same article fixes the boundaries of the state only by the 1:5000 plan annexed to the Treaty as Allegato I, and the Treaty gives no description of them in words. What a visitor meets in the square is the queue for the basilica: the Fabbrica di San Pietro places the security checks by the Italian State Police in the right hemicycle, looking towards the basilica.

faq.question: Do I need a ticket for St Peter's Basilica?
faq.answer: No. The Fabbrica di San Pietro states that the basilica can still be entered without a reservation, from the ordinary entrance in St Peter's Square, and that entry is free. Access begins with security checks by the Italian State Police, whose stations are in the right hemicycle of the square looking towards the basilica. The dome is a separate ticket: the Fabbrica's booking portal lists the dome with stairs, including the basilica, at 17 euro, and the dome with lift at 22 euro. With stairs it is 231 steps to the terrace and 320 more to the top, 551 in all; with the lift, 320 steps remain.

faq.question: When are the Vatican Museums free, and where do I buy a ticket?
faq.answer: The Museums give free entry on the last Sunday of the month, 09.00 to 14.00 with final entry at 12.30, except where that Sunday falls on Easter Sunday, 29 June, 25 December, 26 December or 31 December. Children under 7 enter free, as do directors of museum institutions and heritage bodies, ICOM and ICOMOS card holders, and university teachers in archaeology, art history, architecture and ethnology on written request. Visitors with certified invalidity of at least 67 per cent, and holders of the European Disability Card, enter free and are guaranteed priority entry without queuing, with a companion where the visitor is not self-sufficient; the permit is issued on the day at the Special Permits or Welcome Desk in the entrance hall. The Museums state that tickets are sold online through tickets.museivaticani.va and warn that lookalike domains charge higher prices.

faq.question: Can I get into the Vatican Gardens or the necropolises?
faq.answer: The Vatican Gardens are seen on a booked tour, sold by the Museums as a separate ticket category, and the dress code applies to them. The Necropolis of the Via Triumphalis is also a Museums ticket, and the Museums list it as closed from 15 July to 3 September. The Vatican Necropolis beneath the basilica is a different site altogether, run by the Fabbrica di San Pietro: it is visited by request, arranged through the Fabbrica.

faq.question: How do I get tickets for a papal audience?
faq.answer: The Holy See states that tickets for the General Audiences and the Holy Father's liturgical celebrations are always free of charge. Lay faithful request them from the Prefecture of the Papal Household; bishops, priests and deacons request them from the Office for the Liturgical Celebrations of the Supreme Pontiff. No day, time or venue is stated by those two offices in public.

faq.question: Which famous Roman churches and palaces are not in Vatican City?
faq.answer: San Giovanni in Laterano, Santa Maria Maggiore, San Paolo fuori le Mura, the Palazzo della Cancelleria, the palace of Propaganda Fide, the Palazzo del Sant'Uffizio and the Palazzo dei Convertendi are Lateran Treaty Art. 15 properties. Art. 15 says of them, in terms, that they form part of the territory of the Italian State, and grants them the immunities that international law gives to the seats of the diplomatic agents of foreign States. A visitor to any of them is on Italian soil and under Italian law. Art. 16 is a different list with a different grant: the Gregorian University, the Biblical, Oriental and Archaeological Institutes, the Russian Seminary, the Lombard College, the two Sant'Apollinare palaces and the clergy retreat house at Santi Giovanni e Paolo have only exemption from taxes and protection from expropriation, and are not extraterritorial.

places.name: St Peter's Basilica
places.address: Piazza San Pietro, 00120 Citta del Vaticano
places.summary: Entry is free and needs no reservation, from the ordinary entrance in St Peter's Square. The Fabbrica di San Pietro describes access as beginning with the security checks by the Italian State Police, whose stations are in the right hemicycle of the square looking towards the basilica. The Fabbrica publishes basilica opening hours of 7.00 am to 8.00 pm from 1 June. Guided tours run Monday to Saturday 09.30 to 17.30, last registration 17.00, and Sundays and Vatican holidays 13.30 to 15.30, last registration 15.00. Worshippers and celebrants have a dedicated route with identification at an indicated entrance gate.
places.history: The Fabbrica records that on 18 April 1506, the Saturday after Easter, Julius II laid the first stone of the new basilica at the site of the present south-west pillar of St Veronica. The master of ceremonies Paride de Grassis describes the pope descending by ladder in pontifical robes into the foundation pit, 7.45 metres deep, laying the marble stone and placing a terracotta vessel holding twelve medals modelled by Cristoforo Foppa, known as Caradosso. The Fabbrica names the architects who followed as Fra' Giovanni Giocondo, Raphael Sanzio, Giuliano da Sangallo, Antonio da Sangallo, Baldassarre Peruzzi, Michelangelo Buonarroti, Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola, Giacomo della Porta and Carlo Maderno, who built the facade between 1608 and 1612. In front of the main altar the Confessio opens on the tomb below, and the altars raised over Constantine's marble casket are those of Gregory the Great, 590 to 604, of Callistus II, 1123, and of Clement VIII, 1594, later covered by Bernini's canopy. The Cathedra Sancti Petri Apostoli is an ancient wooden throne with ivory plaques of the labours of Hercules and ivory friezes of the Carolingian age. Michelangelo sculpted the Pieta in 1498, at twenty-three, for Cardinal Jean de Bilhères Lagraulas, who wanted it for his tomb in the Chapel of the King of France, a chapel no longer standing that stood on the southern flank of the old basilica. The Vatican Mosaic Studio dates from the beginning of the sixteenth century, when Gregory XIII entrusted Girolamo Muziano with the mosaic decoration of the dome of the Gregorian Chapel, 1578 to 1580. In 2026 the Fabbrica di San Pietro held a lecture cycle for the fourth centenary of the basilica's dedication.

places.name: St Peter's Square
places.address: Piazza San Pietro, 00120 Citta del Vaticano
places.summary: The square in front of the basilica. Art. 3 of the Lateran Treaty states that St Peter's Square forms part of Vatican City, and that it continues to be normally open to the public. The security checks for the basilica are in the right hemicycle, looking towards it.
places.history: Bernini built the square for Alexander VII and completed it in 1667, after eleven years' work. The Fabbrica describes an oval space with three centres, 196 by 149 metres, with semicircular colonnades joined to the basilica by arms or closed ambulacra enclosing a trapezoidal area bounded on one side by the facade. The colonnade has 284 columns in four rows, 16 metres high, carrying 140 statues more than three metres high. The Vatican obelisk at the centre came from the circus of Caligula and Nero. A large mosaic copy of the fifteenth-century Mater Ecclesiae icon is in the square; the original is venerated inside the basilica in the Chapel of Our Lady of the Column.

places.name: Dome of St Peter's
places.address: Piazza San Pietro, 00120 Citta del Vaticano
places.summary: The climb is ticketed and booked. With stairs it is 231 steps to the basilica terrace and 320 more to the top, 551 in all; with the lift, which reaches the terrace, 320 steps remain. The Fabbrica gives winter hours of 07.30 to 17.00 for 26 October 2025 to 28 March, and summer hours of 07.00 to 18.00 for 29 March 2026 to 25 October 2026. The Fabbrica's booking portal lists the dome with stairs, including the basilica, at 17 euro, and the dome with lift at 22 euro. It is recommended from age 6, under-18s must be accompanied, it is not wheelchair accessible, no animals are admitted, strollers are left under the portico and there is no cloakroom service at present. Tickets are not refundable, transferable or modifiable, and a full refund is given only where the Holy See cancels for a liturgical celebration or event; the inner ring may be closed for celebrations or organisational reasons.
places.history: Michelangelo conceived the dome and built it to the drum. Giacomo della Porta completed it with Domenico Fontana between 1588 and 1590, and the Fabbrica records that the dome was raised in 22 months, with 800 labourers. It is double-shelled with a cavity, ogival, and slenderer than the initial design. On 18 November 1593 the gilded bronze sphere and cross by Sebastiano Torrigiani were placed on the lantern spire. The ring at the end of the lantern carries the inscription set by Clement VIII, s. petri gloriae sixtvs pp. v. a. mdxc pontif. v, and the frieze at the base of the dome reads tv es petrvs et svper hanc petram aedificabo ecclesiam meam et tibi dabo claves regni caelorvm in blue letters on gold. The mosaics were made by numerous mosaicists under Marcello Provenzale between 1598 and 1613, covering about 3,000 square metres in sixteen wedge-shaped compartments. The Fabbrica gives the height of the inner dome of the lantern as 117 metres, and the cross at the top of the dome as over 133 metres.

places.name: Vatican Grottoes
places.summary: The lower level of St Peter's Basilica, with exits to Largo Braschi on the south and Largo San Gregorio l'Illuminatore on the north.
places.history: The vaults were built between 1590 and 1591 to carry the floor of the Renaissance building, on a design descending from a variation Antonio da Sangallo the Younger presented to Leo X after Raphael's death in 1520. In 1592 Clement VIII Aldobrandini renovated the medieval crypt and named it Clementine. In 1616 and 1617 Paul V built two straight corridors to the Confessio and added the chapels of the Salvatorello, of the Madonna of the Bocciata and of the Madonna of the Partorienti, frescoed with the peribolos by Giovan Battista Ricci da Novara. Under Urban VIII, 1623 to 1644, four oratories dedicated to St Veronica, St Helen, St Longinus and St Andrew were built at the base of the dome pillars, designed by Bernini and decorated by Agostino Ciampelli, Guidobaldi Abbatini and others, each with a spiral staircase up to the basilica. National chapels followed: Irish in 1954, Polish in 1958 and 1982, Lithuanian in 1970, Patron Saints of Europe in 1981 and Mexican in 1992, with the oratory holding the tomb of Pius XII from 1958. In 1979 a large archway was opened in the central part, making the front of the Confessio and the Niche of the Pallia visible.

places.name: Treasury Museum of St Peter's Basilica
places.summary: The Fabbrica di San Pietro's product page states that, due to the continuation of work on the new layout, the Treasure Museum will be temporarily closed. The same page confirms that the basilica itself can still be entered without a reservation, from the ordinary entrance in St Peter's Square.
places.history: The Fabbrica records that the Treasury was born with the basilica and was dispersed repeatedly: by the Visigoths in 410, the Vandals in 455, the Ostrogoths in 545, the Saracens in 830 and 846, the Normans in 1084 and the Landsknechts in 1527, and it was requisitioned under the Jacobin occupation of 1798 and 1799. Custody has been with the Chapter of Saint Peter since the eleventh century. A museum arrangement of two rooms was made in 1909, and a larger transformation was carried out from 1949 by the architect Franco Minissi, aimed at the 1975 Jubilee and built on the principle of the protagonism of the objects.

places.name: Petros eni: Saint Peter's Digital Experience
places.summary: An immersive exhibition in the Octagonal Halls, spaces inside one of the pillars that support the dome. The Fabbrica gives winter hours of 07.30 to 17.00 for 26 October 2025 to 28 March, and summer hours of 07.00 to 18.00 for 29 March 2026 to 25 October 2026, and also sells it combined as Petros eni with the basilica and the dome with lift.
places.history: The Octagonal Halls were restored by the Fabbrica's artisans and opened for the exhibition. It runs on two narrative paths, the origins and construction history of the basilica around the tomb of Peter, and the life of the apostle to his martyrdom, and is built on a 3D digitisation of the basilica made from over 400,000 photographs. The Fabbrica names Microsoft, Iconem, DADADA studio and Processoffice as partners, Orpheo for audiovisual engineering, David Chalmin for the music and Manu Kalve for the scenographic installation, with scientific direction by Pietro Zander, project coordination by Fr Francesco Occhetta and narration by Fr Agnello Stoia.

places.name: Vatican Necropolis
places.summary: The Roman cemetery under St Peter's Basilica, below the level of the Vatican Grottoes and between three and eleven metres below the floor of the central nave. The Vatican Necropolis is visited by request, arranged through the Fabbrica di San Pietro.
places.history: Archaeological explorations began in the early years of the pontificate of Pius XII, 1939 to 1958, and the Fabbrica dates the excavations that reached the tomb to 1939 to 1949. Second-century brick tomb buildings became, in the fourth century, the foundations of the first Petrine basilica: Constantine's builders moved over 40,000 cubic metres of earth to level the Vatican hill and demolished the tops of the tombs, and the Constantinian basilica had five naves divided by 88 columns, its floor level with the Trophy of Gaius. Twenty-two tomb buildings have been unearthed, calculated to have held around 1000 burials, and the inscriptions preserve names of individuals from imperial freedmen families. The Trophy of Gaius, the second-century funerary aedicule recorded by the priest Gaius and reported by Eusebius, survives in the Niche of the Pallia in the Confessio. On a fragment of plaster 3.2 by 5.8 centimetres from the red wall are the Greek letters PETR and ENI, read as Petros eni, Peter is here, or Petros en irene, Peter in peace.

places.name: Vatican Museums
places.summary: Open Monday to Saturday 08.00 to 20.00, final entry 18.00, and on the last Sunday of the month 09.00 to 14.00, final entry 12.30, free, with guided tours on reservation, except where that Sunday falls on Easter Sunday, 29 June, 25 December, 26 December or 31 December. Visitors are asked to leave the halls 30 minutes before closing. Closed on Sundays other than the last of the month, on 1 and 6 January, 11 February, 19 March, 6 April, 1 May, 29 June, 14 and 15 August, 1 November, and 8, 25 and 26 December. The full ticket is 20.00 euro without online booking, or 20.00 plus 5.00 euro for Skip the Line on the official site; reduced 10.00 plus 5.00; schools 5.00 plus 2.00; students, pilgrimages and university institutes 10.00 plus 5.00; seminaries and religious colleges 5.00 plus 2.00. The Museums state that tickets are sold online through tickets.museivaticani.va and warn that lookalike domains charge higher prices; a ticket admits to the Museums and the Sistine Chapel on the day it is issued and is not refundable. General information is on +39 06 69883145 and info.musei@scv.va.
places.history: The Directorate of Museums and Cultural Heritage, which runs the Museums, sits under the Governorate of Vatican City State. Practical rules the Museums publish: a dress code of no sleeveless or low-cut garments, no shorts above the knee, no miniskirts and no hats, applying also to the Sistine Chapel, St Peter's Basilica and the Vatican Gardens; a free and compulsory cloakroom for luggage, rucksacks, knives, scissors, metal tools, medium and large umbrellas, sticks, tripods, video cameras, banners and signs; no alcohol brought in, and no eating or drinking in the exhibition halls; no animals except guide dogs, muzzled and leashed, and certified pet-therapy animals with one day's notice by email; no laser pointers. There are vending machines and refreshment areas with cafeteria, self-service and pizzeria along the route, rest areas with seats in the Courtyard of the Cuirasses, the Courtyard of the Pinacoteca, the Square Garden and the Courtyard of the Pinecone, and a branch of the Vatican Post inside the Museums.

places.name: Sistine Chapel
places.summary: On the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. The Museums ask visitors to keep absolute silence inside; guided groups are given their art-historical commentary before entering, at touch-screen totems outside, and informative panels for individual visitors are in the Courtyard of the Pinecone and the Square Garden. The Conclave for the election of the Supreme Pontiff is held in the chapel.
places.history: The chapel is named for Sixtus IV della Rovere, pontiff from 1471 to 1484, who had the old Cappella Magna restored between 1477 and 1480. The fifteenth-century wall decoration runs false drapes, the Stories of Moses on the south and entrance walls, the Stories of Christ on the north and entrance walls, and portraits of the popes; the painters were Pietro Perugino, Sandro Botticelli, Domenico Ghirlandaio and Cosimo Rosselli, with workshops and assistants among whom the Museums name Biagio di Antonio, Bartolomeo della Gatta and Luca Signorelli, and Pier Matteo d'Amelia painted a starry sky on the ceiling. Work on the frescoes began in 1481 and concluded in 1482, and the marble screen, the choir stalls and the pontifical arms over the door date from the same year. Sixtus IV consecrated the chapel on 15 August 1483, dedicating it to Our Lady of the Assumption. Julius II entrusted the ceiling to Michelangelo in 1508; the work was finished in October 1512 and Julius II inaugurated the chapel with a solemn Mass on the Feast of All Saints, 1 November 1512, with nine central panels of the Stories of Genesis, five Sibyls and seven Prophets between the spandrels, the Miraculous salvation of Israel in the four corner pendentives, and the Ancestors of Christ in the spandrels and lunettes. Clement VII de' Medici commissioned the Last Judgement towards the end of 1533; Michelangelo began it in 1536 under Paul III and completed it in the autumn of 1541, destroying Perugino's altarpiece of the Virgin among the Apostles and the first two episodes of both fresco cycles. In the second half of the sixteenth century Hendrik van den Broeck repainted Ghirlandaio's Resurrection on the entrance wall and Matteo da Lecce repainted Signorelli's Discussion over the body of Moses, which had been damaged when the door collapsed in 1522. The frescoes were restored completely between 1979 and 1999, together with the cantoria, the screen and the arms of Sixtus IV.

places.name: Pinacoteca Vaticana
places.summary: The picture gallery of the Vatican Museums, in its own building on the museum itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. It holds 460 paintings in eighteen rooms, arranged by chronology and school from the Primitives of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries to the nineteenth century; the artists the Museums name include Giotto, Fra Angelico, Melozzo da Forli, Perugino, Raphael, Leonardo, Titian, Veronese, Caravaggio and Crespi.
places.history: Pius VI made a first collection of 118 paintings around 1790, broken up when the Treaty of Tolentino of 1797 sent works to Paris. The idea of a public gallery dates from 1817, after the returns that followed the Congress of Vienna. The present building was designed by Luca Beltrami for Pius XI and inaugurated on 27 October 1932, standing isolated in the nineteenth-century Square Garden and surrounded by avenues so that it could be lit from every side.

places.name: Raphael's Rooms
places.summary: Four rooms on the second floor of the Pontifical Palace, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket.
places.history: Julius II chose the rooms as his residence and his successors used them after him. Raphael Sanzio and his school painted the decoration between 1508 and 1524.

places.name: Borgia Apartment
places.summary: Six rooms in the Apostolic Palace, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. They now hold part of the Collection of Modern and Contemporary Art.
places.history: The rooms were renovated and decorated for Alexander VI, 1492 to 1503: the Room of the Sibyls and the Room of the Creed in the Borgia Tower; the rooms of the Liberal Arts, of the Saints and of the Mysteries in the wing built by Nicholas V, 1447 to 1455, and called the secret rooms in the diary of Johannes Burckhardt; and the Room of the Pontiffs in the older wing built by Nicholas III, 1277 to 1280. Bernardino di Betto, Pinturicchio, carried out the decoration rapidly between the autumn of 1492 and the beginning of 1494 with a team including Piermatteo d'Amelia, Benedetto Bonfigli, Pietro d'Andrea and Antonio da Viterbo, il Pastura, with Bartolomeo di Giovanni and Raffaellino del Garbo on recent attributions. The technique was largely dry paint on plaster and glue rather than true fresco, as recent restoration confirmed. No contract survives, but a letter of 29 March 1493 from Alexander VI to Orvieto records Pinturicchio's transfer to the Vatican. Julius II left the apartment in 1503 and moved a floor up, and Leo XIII opened it to the public at the end of the 1800s after restoration.

places.name: Collection of Modern and Contemporary Art
places.summary: Around 8,000 works, of which the displayed selection runs from the Borgia Apartment to the Sistine Chapel, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. The artists the Museums name include Van Gogh, Bacon, Chagall, Carra, de Chirico, Manzu, Capogrossi, Fontana, Burri and Matisse.
places.history: Paul VI inaugurated the collection on 23 June 1973, following his address to artists in the Sistine Chapel on 7 May 1964. It was assembled over about ten years by his secretary Msgr Pasquale Macchi, on a nucleus of nineteenth-century works that had entered the Pinacoteca in the late 1950s under Pius XII. A Matisse room opened in 2011, holding works relating to the Vence Chapel that came into the collections in 1980 by gift of Pierre Matisse.

places.name: Gregorian Egyptian Museum
places.summary: Nine rooms and a hemicycle opening onto the terrace of the Niche of the Pinecone, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. It is strong in material from Roman Egypt and Egyptianising Rome, including the statuary group from the Horti Sallustiani, now in the hemicycle, and items from Hadrian's Villa at Tivoli; the final three rooms hold Ancient Near Eastern material acquired in the 1970s.
places.history: Gregory XVI founded the museum in 1839, in rooms taken from the apartment of Pius IV in the Belvedere Palace of Innocent VIII. The Barnabite Fr Luigi Ungarelli, a disciple of Ippolito Rosellini, first curated it, and the architectural and wall decoration evokes the Nile.

places.name: Gregorian Etruscan Museum
places.summary: On the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. It covers the Iron Age of the ninth century BC to the convergence with Rome in the first century BC, and its Antiquarium Romanum section runs to the fifth century AD. Bramante's double-helix staircase, begun in 1512, is visible from inside the museum.
places.history: Gregory XVI founded the museum and it was inaugurated on 2 February 1837. Later acquisitions came from Falcioni in 1898, Benedetto Guglielmi in 1935, Mario Astarita in 1967 and Giacinto Guglielmi in 1987. It occupies the Palazzetto del Belvedere of Innocent VIII Cibo, 1484 to 1492, designed by Pollaiolo, and the apartment of the Tor dei Venti of Pius IV Medici, 1559 to 1565, begun by Michelangelo and Girolamo da Carpi and finished by Pirro Ligorio. The sixteenth-century fresco cycles are by Federico Barocci and Federico Zuccari, 1563, and Santi di Tito and Niccolo Circignani delle Pomarance, 1564.

places.name: Pio Clementino Museum
places.summary: The classical sculpture museum of the Vatican Museums, in and beside the Belvedere Palace of Innocent VIII, on the museum itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket.
places.history: The nucleus is the collection of Julius II, 1503 to 1513, in the Cortile delle Statue, today the Octagonal Court. The museum is named for Clement XIV Ganganelli, 1769 to 1774, and Pius VI Braschi, 1775 to 1799, and its neo-classical architecture is the work of Alessandro Dori, Michelangelo Simonetti and Giuseppe Camporese. Principal works went to Paris under the Treaty of Tolentino of 1797 and most were recovered after the Congress of Vienna of 1815, through the diplomacy of Antonio Canova.

places.name: Chiaramonti Museum, the Braccio Nuovo and the Lapidary Gallery
places.summary: Sculpture and inscriptions set out in the long loggia that joins the Belvedere palace to the Vatican palaces, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. Works the Museums name here are Heracles with the infant Telephos, the Gradiva, the Augustus of Prima Porta, the Nile and the Peacocks.
places.history: The museum is named for Pius VII Chiaramonti. The New Wing, the Braccio Nuovo, was built when the works confiscated by Napoleon returned from France and the pontifical collections were re-ordered.

places.name: Gallery of the Geographical Maps
places.summary: A gallery 120 metres long and 6 metres wide, hung with forty cartographic representations of the Italian territories and the dominions of the Church, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. Thirty-two maps of territories are aligned north to south and divided conceptually by the Apennines, and eight narrower maps at the ends show the Siege of Malta, the Battle of Lepanto, Elba, the Tremiti Islands and the ports of Civitavecchia, Genoa, Venice and Ancona. The ceiling carries 51 painted panels in stucco frames.
places.history: Gregory XIII wanted the gallery, and Ottaviano Nonni, il Mascherino, built it between 1578 and 1580. A large team coordinated by Girolamo Muziano and Cesare Nebbia frescoed it in under two years, to an iconographic programme by the Perugian Dominican Egnazio Danti, cosmographer, astronomer and mathematician.

places.name: Gallery of the Tapestries
places.summary: On the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. The series the Museums name are the Life of Christ, by the New School, and the Life of Urban VIII Barberini.
places.history: The tapestries were originally shown in two sections; the present gallery was formed between 1788 and 1789 under Pius VI Braschi.

places.name: Gregoriano Profano Museum
places.summary: Greek and Roman sculpture on the Vatican Museums itinerary, covered by the Museums ticket. The works the Museums name include marble from the Parthenon, the Athena and Marsyas, the Asarotos oikos mosaic, the Chiaramonti Niobid, a Julius Caesar, the reliefs from the Palazzo della Cancelleria, material from the Mausoleum of the Haterii and a mosaic from the Baths of Caracalla.
places.history: Gregory XVI Cappellari founded the museum in the Lateran Apostolic Palace on 16 May 1844, and the collection was later moved into the Vatican Museums.

places.name: Pius-Christian Museum
places.summary: Material from the Christian communities of the first centuries, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. The Museums name the Good Shepherd and Jonah, strigilated sarcophagi, continuous-frieze sarcophagi, the mosaics of Ciriaca, double-register and column sarcophagi, and a Nativity and Epiphany.
places.history: Pius IX founded the museum in 1854, in the Lateran Palace, to hold evidence of the Christian communities of the first centuries; the collection was later moved into the Vatican Museums.

places.name: Jewish Lapidarium
places.summary: A collection of ancient inscriptions transferred from the Lateran Palace, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket. Among the inscriptions the Museums name are those of Primitiva, Salutia, Ioustos, Ioudas and Regina.

places.name: Carriage Pavilion
places.summary: Carriages, cars and sedan chairs on the Vatican Museums itinerary, covered by the Museums ticket. Besides the Grand Gala Berlin, the Museums list the Berlin of Cardinal Luciano Luigi Bonaparte, a gala Berlin with throne, the travelling carriage of Ferdinand II, a landau, the sedan chairs of Leo XIII and John XXIII, a Graham Paige Type 837, a Citroen Lictoria C6, a Mercedes-Benz 460 Nurburg limousine, a Mercedes-Benz 300 SEL limousine, a Fiat 1107 Nuova Campagnola, papamobiles, a Volkswagen Type 1 Beetle, a Renault 4 and the steering wheel of a Ferrari Formula 1 MT 867/B.
places.history: Paul VI inaugurated the pavilion on 19 April 1973. Its core is the Grand Gala Berlin, built in Rome in 1826.

places.name: Ethnological Museum Anima Mundi
places.summary: The ethnological collections of the Vatican Museums, now numbering over 80,000 artefacts, on the museum itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket.
places.history: The origin was the Vatican Missionary Exposition, inaugurated on 24 December 1924 and closed on 9 January 1926, which showed over 100,000 works in twenty-six pavilions. Pius XI founded the Ethnological Museum on 12 November 1926 and directed it to Fr Wilhelm Schmidt SVD, 1868 to 1954; the Missionary Ethnological Museum was inaugurated at St John Lateran on 21 December 1927 with about 80,000 works, and was enriched from 1928 with material from the Museo Borgiano of Propaganda Fide, some of it from the collection of Cardinal Stefano Borgia, 1731 to 1804. It closed on 1 February 1963, after John XXIII assigned the Lateran palace to the diocese of Rome, and the collection was stored at Palazzo San Callisto until a new venue opened inside the Vatican Museums in 1973 under Paul VI, designed by Fr Jozef Penkowski SVD, 1930 to 2006, with the Passarelli studio. A conservation programme ran from 1996 to 2009 under Don Roberto Zagnoli, 1938 to 2020, and the Ethnological Materials Laboratory was founded in 2001, coordinated by Stefania Pandozy to 2023 and then by Catherine Riviere. The Asia section part-opened for the Museums' fifth centenary, 1506 to 2006. The redisplay ran from 2009 to 2023 under Fr Nicola Mapelli, with the permanent display The Way of the Sea in 2010, Anima Mundi opening in 2019 with Mater Amazonia and the Oceania area, and the Americas and Africa completed in 2022. Nadia Fiussello has been curator since August 2024.

places.name: Niccoline Chapel
places.summary: A small chapel in the Apostolic Palace, near Raphael's loggias, on the Vatican Museums itinerary and covered by the Museums ticket.
places.history: It is named for Nicholas V, Tommaso Parentucelli, 1447 to 1455, who had it built in the top two floors of a tower raised under Innocent III. Fra Angelico decorated it, and two payments of February and March 1448 date the work: two registers run the perimeter with the lives of St Stephen and St Lawrence, the ceiling carries the Four Evangelists in four sail sections, and eight Doctors of the Church stand in niches on the framing arches. The Museums' timeline records a restoration in 1995 and 1996.

places.name: Necropolis of the Via Triumphalis
places.summary: A Roman burial ground on the terraced slopes beside the stretch of the Via Triumphalis nearest the city, bordering the Vatican Hill. The Museums sell it as a separate ticket category, and their table of temporary and extraordinary closures gives it as closed from 15 July to 3 September. It is a different site from the Vatican Necropolis under St Peter's Basilica, which the Fabbrica di San Pietro runs.
places.history: The tombs are collective and individual, set along paths and squares, and many carry inscribed funerary stelae naming the dead, largely people from the middle and lower ranks of imperial Roman society.

places.name: Vatican Gardens
places.summary: About 22 hectares, roughly half the territory of the state. They are seen on a booked tour, sold by the Vatican Museums as a separate ticket category, and the Museums' dress code applies. The itinerary the Museums publish names the Italian Garden, the Fountain of the Eagle, the Fountain of the Zitella, the Casina of Pius IV, Our Lady of the Watch, the Lourdes Grotto, Saint John's Tower, the Jubilee 2000 Bell, a bronze statue of Saint Peter and the Square Garden.
places.history: The gardens go back to 1279 and the pontificate of Nicholas III, 1277 to 1280, who moved the papal residence from the Lateran to the Vatican and had a pomerium, a pratellum and a viridarium planted inside his new walls on Mons Saccorum; the Governorate records that the stone inscription of this planting is now on the Capitol. A Belvedere palace of delights followed under Innocent VIII, 1484 to 1492, and Bramante's Belvedere courtyard under Julius II. Pirro Ligorio, 1512 or 1513 to 1583, built the Casina with its loggia for Pius IV by 1565. Pius V added exotic and rare plants collected by the botanist Michele Mercati and the Bolognese scholar Ulisse Aldrovandi, and Mercati laid out the geometric flowerbeds. The restoration of Trajan's aqueduct in the early seventeenth century allowed the fountains to run. Napoleon's troops plundered much of the gardens at the end of the eighteenth century, and Gregory XVI, 1831 to 1846, commissioned a renovation that Gaetano Moroni described in his Dizionario di erudizione storico-ecclesiastica, 1840 to 1861. Among the trees are nineteenth-century sculptures: a Saint Peter in chains by Maria Luisa Amalia Dupre, 1842 to 1928, given in 1887, and a bronze Saint Alpino stopping Attila by Jean Ernest Boutellier, 1851 to 1916, given in 1887 and 1888. After 1929 the architect Giuseppe Momo, 1875 to 1940, with the botanist Giovanni Nicolini, laid out the present gardens over four years.

places.name: Vatican Apostolic Library
places.summary: A research library, not a visitor site. The Library states that it does not offer regular public visits, and that access to its historic and monumental spaces may be granted on an occasional basis in conjunction with special events and institutional initiatives. Its reading rooms open Monday to Friday from 09.00 to 17.20, and admission is for researchers and scholars with appropriate qualifications or relevant scientific publications, teachers and researchers at universities and other institutes of higher education, graduates pursuing doctoral research and, exceptionally, undergraduates who can show they need material available only here. The contact address is bav@vatlib.it.
places.history: The Library gives its holdings as approximately 180,000 manuscripts and archival documents, around 2,000,000 printed books, about 8,300 incunabula, approximately 300,000 coins and medals, over 100,000 graphic works of prints, drawings and engraved plates, and more than 150,000 photographs. It describes itself as specialising in philological and historical disciplines and, more broadly, in theological, legal and scientific fields, and as dedicated to scholarly research on the direct study of manuscripts, printed books, coins and medals, prints, and graphic and cartographic materials. By papal decree, in the Library's own words, it is open to qualified scholars and researchers, regardless of religion, origin, or cultural background.

places.name: Vatican Apostolic Archive
places.summary: The Archive's rooms are along the braccio di Pio IV of the Apostolic Palace, adjacent to the Salone Sistino, on the Piano Nobile. Research is free of charge and open to qualified scholars holding a laurea magistrale or equivalent, and for clergy a licentiate or doctorate; consultation is currently permitted for documents up to and including the pontificate of Pius XII, October 1958. It opens to scholars Monday and Tuesday 08.00 to 16.15 and Wednesday to Friday 08.00 to 12.45, with admission cards issued by the Segreteria Accettazioni Monday and Tuesday 08.00 to 12.00 and Wednesday to Friday 08.00 to 10.30. The study-room rules are strict: no bags, briefcases or laptop cases, no ballpoint or fountain pens or markers, no cameras, portable scanners or wearable technology with lenses or recording sensors, including smart glasses and digital watches, no food or drink, phones on silent and used only outdoors in the courtyard, sober dress including in summer, and silence in the study rooms.
places.history: Paul V created the Novum Archivum in the Apostolic Palace in 1611, concentrating registers from the Vatican Library, the Camera Apostolica and the archive of Castel Sant'Angelo in the Sala Paolina; on 31 January 1612 he appointed Baldassarre Ansidei custodian, and the Archive's history formally begins there. The material moved to the three Piano Nobile rooms in 1613 and 1614. Urban VIII established its autonomy from the Library on 23 July 1630. The name Archivio Segreto Vaticano appears in 1646, in a general index by the prefect Costanzo Centofiorini. Alexander VII assigned the floor above to the Secretariat of State archive in 1660. In 1798 the archive of Castel Sant'Angelo was moved in. Napoleon confiscated the papal archives in 1810, about 3,239 crates leaving Rome, with heavy losses on the return. Leo XIII opened the Archive to scholars of every country and religion in 1881. The Bunker depositories beneath the Cortile della Pigna were built on two floors, with a capacity of 31,000 cubic metres and 43 linear kilometres of shelving. On 22 October 2019, by the motu proprio L'esperienza storica, Francis replaced the title Archivio Segreto Vaticano with the older name Archivio Apostolico Vaticano. The Archive holds over 600 fondi, grouped as curial offices, over 75 pontifical diplomatic representations from the early sixteenth to the twentieth century, family and personal archives including Boncompagni-Ludovisi, Borghese, Della Valle-Del Bufalo, Patrizi-Montoro, Ruspoli-Marescotti and Rospigliosi, with the Fondo Albani, Carpegna and Pio, councils and synods including the complete archives of Vatican I and Vatican II and a large part of Trent, religious orders and archconfraternities, and miscellaneous collections.

entries.name: St Peter's Basilica
entries.note: Free and unreserved, from the ordinary entrance in the square; Julius II laid the first stone on 18 April 1506 and Maderno built the facade between 1608 and 1612.

entries.name: St Peter's Square
entries.note: Bernini finished it in 1667 after eleven years: an oval space with three centres, 196 by 149 metres, with 284 columns in four rows carrying 140 statues.

entries.name: Dome of St Peter's
entries.note: 231 steps to the terrace and 320 more to the top, 551 in all, or 320 with the lift; 17 euro with stairs and 22 euro with lift, both including the basilica.

entries.name: Vatican Grottoes
entries.note: Vaults of 1590 and 1591 under the basilica floor, with Bernini's four oratories at the base of the dome pillars and the tomb of Pius XII from 1958.

entries.name: Vatican Necropolis
entries.note: Three to eleven metres below the nave floor, visited by request through the Fabbrica di San Pietro; 22 tomb buildings and around 1000 burials have been unearthed.

entries.name: Vatican Museums
entries.note: Monday to Saturday 08.00 to 20.00, final entry 18.00, and free on the last Sunday of the month from 09.00 to 14.00, final entry 12.30.

entries.name: Buying a Vatican Museums ticket
entries.note: The Museums sell tickets online through tickets.museivaticani.va and warn that lookalike domains charge more; a ticket is valid on its day of issue and is not refundable.

entries.name: Sistine Chapel
entries.note: Michelangelo's ceiling was inaugurated on 1 November 1512 and the Last Judgement finished in the autumn of 1541; visitors are asked to keep silence inside.

entries.name: Gallery of the Geographical Maps
entries.note: 120 metres long and 6 metres wide, hung with forty maps painted between 1578 and 1580 to Egnazio Danti's programme, under a ceiling of 51 panels.

entries.name: Pinacoteca Vaticana
entries.note: 460 paintings in eighteen rooms, from the Primitives to the nineteenth century, in Luca Beltrami's building inaugurated on 27 October 1932.

entries.name: Raphael's Rooms
entries.note: Julius II's residence on the second floor of the Pontifical Palace, painted by Raphael and his school between 1508 and 1524.

entries.name: Necropolis of the Via Triumphalis
entries.note: A Roman burial ground on terraced slopes beside the road, sold as its own Museums ticket and given as closed from 15 July to 3 September.

entries.name: Vatican Gardens
entries.note: About 22 hectares, half the territory, seen on a booked tour sold as a separate Museums ticket; the dress code applies here too.

entries.name: Vatican Apostolic Library
entries.note: A working research library rather than a visitor site: it states that it does not offer regular public visits, and its reading rooms open Monday to Friday 09.00 to 17.20.
